title: From breadboard to schematic
summary: Draw the season's AND gate as a real schematic, read one number off an LED datasheet, then measure the LED's current for three resistor values and check it against a prediction.
materials: breadboard starter kit and electronics add-on pack
micro:bit v2 and micro USB cable
laptop, for a datasheet search, and KiCad or a paper circuit-symbol sheet (free, at https://www.kicad.org)

figure.alt: A schematic loop connects the battery to two buttons in series, then a resistor, then the LED, and back down to the battery, matching the order battery, button, button, resistor, LED used in the AND gate circuit.

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop opens the electronics half of the season: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: a breadboard photo shows where wires sit, but not why the circuit works. Can the same circuit be drawn as a plan anyone could rebuild from, wires and all?

Imagine: a schematic, a drawing using proper symbols instead of a photo. A zigzag stands for a resistor, a triangle with an arrow for the LED, two parallel lines for the battery.

Plan: pick the week 1 AND gate from earlier in the season to redraw. On graph paper, or in KiCad at https://www.kicad.org, sketch the symbols first without wiring them. Then connect them in the same order the real circuit follows: battery, button, button, resistor, LED, back to battery.

figure.alt: Three resistor pipes of different widths represent 220, 330 and 1000 ohms. The widest pipe, 220 ohms, is predicted to pass about six milliamps, the middle pipe, 330 ohms, about four milliamps, and the narrowest pipe, 1000 ohms, about one point three milliamps: a wider pipe lets more current through.

steps.title: The resistor is a narrow pipe you can predict
steps.body:
A resistor is a narrow pipe: the narrower it is, the less current gets through for the same push. That push comes from the supply voltage. An LED eats a fixed slice of it, usually about 2 volts for a standard red LED, before the resistor gets whatever is left.

The micro:bit's 3V pin actually supplies about 3.3 volts. With that supply and a 2 volt LED, the leftover 1.3 volts falls across the resistor, and current equals that leftover voltage divided by the resistance. A 330 ohm resistor gives about 4 milliamps, and a smaller 220 ohm resistor lets through more, about 6 milliamps. A bigger 1000 ohm resistor lets through less, about 1.3 milliamps.

That is a prediction, not a fact yet. Real LEDs and real resistors are not exactly their labelled numbers, so the multimeter gets the final say, and today it will.

figure.alt: The micro:bit's 3V pin feeds through the multimeter wired in series, then a resistor, then the LED, and back down to the ground pin, forming the loop used to measure current for each resistor value.

steps.title: Datasheet, then measure three resistors
steps.body:
Search for a datasheet for a standard 5 millimetre red LED and find the row for its maximum forward current, usually listed near 20 milliamps for an ordinary indicator LED. Write that one number down; it is the ceiling you must always stay under, and every resistor tested today keeps the current well below it.

Build the circuit on the breadboard: micro:bit 3V pin, one resistor, the LED, back to the micro:bit's ground pin. Before measuring, set the multimeter to read current and break the loop to insert it in series, red probe toward the 3V pin and black probe toward the LED.

Measure the current for the 220, 330 and 1000 ohm resistors, one at a time, swapping only the resistor between readings. Compare each measured number with the prediction from the science step.
checklist: One real number was read from an LED datasheet and written down
The multimeter was wired in series in the loop, not across two points
Current measured for all three resistor values, only the resistor changing each time
Every measured current sat close to its prediction and well under the datasheet's maximum

steps.title: Resistor versus predicted and measured current
steps.body:
The supply, the LED and the wiring stay the same for every row. Only the resistor changes, and each one is read on the multimeter three times, with the middle reading written down.

Three rows, one per resistor value. For each row, write the resistor in ohms, the predicted current in milliamps from the science step, and the measured current in milliamps.
steps.question: Which resistor let through the least current, and how many milliamps less was it than the smallest resistor?

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body:
One line for each thing that did not work the first time and what you tried. Classics this week: the multimeter set to measure voltage instead of current, giving a reading that answers the wrong question.

Also watch for the meter wired across the LED instead of broken into the loop. And a measured current noticeably lower than predicted is usually just the resistor's true value drifting a little from its label.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photo or file of the schematic drawing with real symbols, next to a photo of the multimeter reading current in the loop, and your table of three predicted versus measured currents

extras.title: A two-LED warning light
extras.body:
1. Wire a second LED and resistor branch onto the breadboard, in parallel with the first, so both LEDs share the same battery.

2. Give the new branch a different resistor value from the first, say 220 ohm next to the first branch's 330 ohm.

3. Predict which LED will glow brighter before turning the power on, using the same reasoning as the science step.

4. Measure the current in each branch separately with the multimeter, one branch at a time.

Notice which LED actually looks brighter and whether the branch with more current matches it. A brighter LED and a higher measured current should point at the same resistor every time.
